title: How To Handle A Bossy Colleague
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to the familiar workplace problem of a pushy colleague who constantly pressures a teacher to do things their way, Linsin argues that nothing changes until the teacher sets a firm verbal boundary. His specific tactic is to calmly and respectfully repeat a single phrase, 'No, I'm not going to do that,' whenever pressured, and if pressed further, to add only 'It's a good idea, but not right for me' before changing the subject. He acknowledges this takes courage, especially with a colleague who has long had influence, but argues the discomfort lasts only minutes while the payoff is lasting: the bossy colleague eases off, and often comes to respect the teacher more as an independent, competent professional. The piece closes by stressing that boundary-setting should be paired with continued warmth and normal collegiality, not coldness or a desire to teach the other person a lesson.
points: Set a boundary with a bossy colleague by calmly, respectfully repeating a single fixed phrase: 'No, I'm not going to do that.'
If pressed for a reason, give only one line — 'It's a good idea, but not right for me' — then change the subject rather than explaining further.
The discomfort of standing your ground lasts only a few minutes; the alternative is ongoing stress that can push a teacher toward quitting.
A colleague who is pushed back on, even if briefly offended, often comes to respect the teacher more as competent and independent.
Maintain warmth after setting the boundary — stay friendly, ask about their weekend — the goal is a boundary, not a punishment or a lesson taught.
quotes: We’ve all been annoyed by the bossy colleague who is constantly giving advice and pushing you to do things their way.
It’s to calmly and respectfully repeat the same phrase whenever they begin pressuring you to do (or teach) anything you don’t want to do.
Now, if they follow up by asking why not, just say “It’s a good idea, but not right for me.” There is no need to go on and on or explain further.
You have to stand up for yourself in this profession to avoid the kind of stress that will cause you to quit teaching.
Speaking up can feel awkward and the last thing you want to do. But the discomfort is only for a few minutes then gone forever.
They’ll begin to view you as a strong, independent, and competent teacher who doesn’t need their constant input.
